claims.text: Tribological performance initially improves as ambient temperature rises.
The temperature-driven improvement is caused by a stable, continuous tribo-oxidation film that shields the substrate from direct mechanical contact.
Wear will degrade sharply above a critical temperature because the oxide film becomes mechanically unstable.
A thermally induced FCC-to-HCP transition can reduce ductility, promote cracking, and sharply degrade wear resistance.
The initial material is an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 or similar HEA coating on a transition-metal matrix.
The coating is initially single-phase FCC or BCC at ambient temperature.
At 800-900°C, tribo-oxidation can produce a stable, nearly continuous oxide film and reduce wear depth.
At room temperature and lower elevated temperatures, oxide layers are rough, inhomogeneous, and continuously removed, resulting in abrasive wear.
CoCrFeMnNi can undergo a sluggish and irreversible FCC-to-HCP transformation under high pressure.
Temperature shifts can favor an FCC-to-HCP transition in CoCrFeMnNi.
Phase instability associated with an FCC/HCP transition induces stress concentrations and interfacial cracking.
Wear rate follows a non-monotonic temperature dependence, with high wear at room temperature and a minimum at 800-900°C.
Wear rate rises sharply at temperatures above the 800-900°C optimum.
Room-temperature wear is relatively high because rough, inhomogeneous oxides are continuously removed.
The oxide-film transition occurs near 800°C, with rough and inhomogeneous oxide below this temperature and a continuous protective film at 800-900°C.
A thermodynamically driven matrix phase transition at high operating temperature defines an upper degradation boundary.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between a coating and metallic substrate can produce interfacial cracks and compromise oxidation resistance.
The phase-instability threshold for the proposed coating composition is unknown because the cited transition evidence concerns other alloy systems and high-pressure conditions.
Specific wear rate, oxide continuity, FCC/HCP phase fraction, and interfacial cracking are measurable variables that can test the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis frames degradation as occurring when temperature exceeds an upper boundary, but the boundary field also defines degraded, rough oxide behavior as occurring below approximately 800°C. No supported upper-temperature transition from stable to unstable oxide is identified.

The proposed high-temperature FCC-to-HCP pathway conflicts with the cited phase behavior: the evidence reports pressure-induced FCC-to-HCP at room temperature and the inverse HCP-to-FCC transition upon heating.

The predicted outcome places the wear minimum at 800-900°C, but the falsification rule says that wear at 900°C being lower than at 600°C would falsify the hypothesis. That result would instead be consistent with the stated 800-900°C optimum and protective-oxide mechanism.
The proposed test range ends at 900°C, while the predicted sharp degradation is placed after the 800-900°C optimum. The design therefore may not cross the claimed upper degradation boundary.
